A $25 million federal grant will help bring a new generation of transportation technology to downtown Chattanooga, with UTC playing a central role in research, education and workforce development.
 The grant, awarded to CARTA through the U.S. Department of Transportation’s BUILD program, will support autonomous electric shuttles and the infrastructure needed to operate them. A new Live-Learning Lab will give UTC students and faculty the opportunity to study and develop autonomous transportation technology alongside an operating transit system, building on research from UTC’s Center for Urban Informatics and Progress.
 The project will also help prepare students for careers in autonomous systems, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity and connected infrastructure.
 Read the full story: https://blog.utc.edu/…/utc-to-play-key-role-in-25-million-…/

Official development assistance (ODA), which is government aid that promotes and specifically targets the economic development and welfare of developing countries, remains a core component of development co-operation, but it is one part of a broader financing landscape. Commercial money channelled towards sustainable development objectives is increasingly shaping private flows and investment.
 The 2026 #OECD Development Co-operation Profiles introduce a new feature that helps users situate and compare ODA in partner countries’ wider finance landscape.
 You can use the platform to:
 ➡️ Compare total flows across providers and over time
 ➡️ Explore how ODA, private flows and other sources contribute to development finance
 ➡️ Explore the evolution of ODA, private flows and other financing components by provider
 ➡️ Understand what is driving changes in financing patterns
 Access the OECD Development Co-operation Profiles: https://brnw.ch/21x5sSL
 #DCprofiles2026 #OECDdevelopment

Reproductive health and infectious disease control face the largest projected cuts in official development assistance (O...
items.content_text:
Reproductive health and infectious disease control face the largest projected cuts in official development assistance (ODA).
 ODA is financial support from governments promoting the economic development and welfare of developing countries.
 #OECD projections show that some of the most critical areas of health are expected to experience the sharpest reductions in bilateral ODA between 2024 and 2026.
 ➡️ Population and reproductive health, including HIV/AIDS and other sexually transmitted disease control, is projected to face the largest reduction in funding by volume, with cuts more than ten times larger than the next most-affected health area.
 ➡️ Funding for the control of malaria and tuberculosis is projected to decline by 60% and 57% respectively, the largest percentage reductions among health programmes.
 As outbreaks of infectious diseases become more frequent and widespread, these reductions raise concerns about countries' ability to prevent, detect and respond to future health crises. The cuts to reproductive health programmes are also likely to have a disproportionate impact on women.
 Explore the latest data on ODA for health: https://brnw.ch/21x5sxJ
 #ODA2026 #OECDdevelopment

Yesterday, students at Alpine Crest Elementary took part in the Apex Fun Run! 🏃‍♀️🏃‍♂️🎉

The Apex Fun Run is a 30-minute event that gets kids moving, cheering each other on, and having fun while building teamwork and school spirit. Students also help raise money for their school, with family and friends making pledges based on the number of laps they complete.

And they really got their steps in! Elementary students typically average 26–36 laps during the 30-minute run. But they don’t just run the whole time! To keep things fun, different types of laps are mixed in, including skipping and “swimming” laps, along with girls-only and boys-only laps. 🏊‍♀️🏊‍♂️ It kept everyone moving, laughing, and cheering each other on from start to finish! 💙

We asked everyone: What was your key takeaway from today? And this is what they had to say! 🎥

Last week, Chattanooga 2.0 brought together community leaders, educators, youth-serving organizations, local partners, and young people for the Chattanooga-Hamilton County Adolescent Development Learning Series. The two-day gathering focused on understanding adolescent development and exploring what young people need to thrive.

The event also launched "Thriving Adolescence," Chattanooga 2.0’s newest Big Bet—a community-wide commitment to helping young people ages 10–24 feel supported, connected, and empowered to pursue their futures.

The Learning Series reminded us that helping young people thrive is a shared responsibility. Thank you to everyone who continues to support Chattanooga 2.0 and its efforts to make Hamilton County a better place for our youth and everyone who calls this community home.

Here’s to building a stronger, more connected Hamilton County where every young person has the opportunity to thrive! 🌟

items.title: $25 million will be invested into Chattanooga's public transportation, thanks to funding from the FY26 BUILD grant from...
items.content_text:
$25 million will be invested into Chattanooga's public transportation, thanks to funding from the FY26 BUILD grant from the US Department of Transportation. Not only will this project replace and modernize CARTA's downtown shuttle fleet with autonomous shuttles, but it will develop the Mobility & Innovation Command Center (located at the Shuttle Park South garage).
 The shuttles, operated by Beep for the first three years, will communicate directly with traffic signals and roadside infrastructure along the corridor. This is also a milestone for workforce development — right next door, UTC will create their own center for an autonomous system as a live-learning lab, establishing curriculum and a pipeline for education and jobs in this industry in direct partnership with CARTA.

Great news for Chattanooga! Chattanooga Area Regional Transportation Authority announced a $25 million federal grant to bring 𝐚𝐮𝐭𝐨𝐧𝐨𝐦𝐨𝐮𝐬 𝐞𝐥𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐜 𝐬𝐡𝐮𝐭𝐭𝐥𝐞𝐬 to downtown Chattanooga.
 This project is a great example of what makes our community strong: bringing together transportation, technology, workforce development and tourism to enhance the visitor experience and strengthen our destination. 
 We're excited to see what's next!
 #VisitChatt #Chattanooga
A $25 MILLION INVESTMENT IN THE FUTURE OF CHATTANOOGA!
 Today, CARTA announced the largest competitive grant award in our history: $25 million through the U.S. Department of Transportation’s FY2026 BUILD Grant program.
 This investment is about so much more than autonomous vehicles. It’s about building the people, infrastructure, technology, and expertise Chattanooga needs to lead the future of transportation.
 Here at Shuttle Park South, CARTA and UTC will create a permanent Mobility & Innovation Command Center to oversee and support the next generation of transit technology.
 A new Live-Learning Lab will connect technology with education, giving students, researchers, and CARTA employees opportunities to learn and develop skills in autonomous systems, transportation technology, AI, data, cybersecurity, and more.
 Building on the City of Chattanooga and UTC’s SMART Grant work and EPB’s technology infrastructure, this project will help create a more connected and innovative transportation system.
 Most importantly, we’re not just bringing the future of transportation to Chattanooga and we’re preparing Chattanoogans to lead it.
 Over the next three years, CARTA and our partners will build the infrastructure, develop the workforce, test new technology, and create expertise that can serve our community for decades to come.

items.content_text:
Bilateral official development assistance (ODA) for health is projected to fall to its lowest level in almost two decades.
 ODA is financial support from governments promoting the economic development and welfare of developing countries.
 #OECD projections show that bilateral ODA for health could decline by 29-46% between 2024 and 2026, equivalent to a reduction of USD 5-8 billion. This would bring support back to levels not seen since 2008.
 The decline follows the sharp increase in health ODA during the COVID-19 pandemic. By 2026, funding is projected to be 63% below its 2022 peak, with further reductions expected beyond 2026 as major providers continue to implement multi-year cuts.
 Health was the third-largest sector for bilateral ODA in 2024, receiving USD 17.6 billion, after humanitarian aid and support to government and civil society. The scale of the projected reductions could therefore have significant implications for countries that rely on external financing to support their health systems. 
 Explore the latest data on ODA for health ➡️ https://brnw.ch/21x5pb1

🚨 WARNING SHOTS FIRED 🚨
 Listen, I try to stay in my lane in the City of Chattanooga, which is in Hamilton County. But today I’m speaking as something else too:
 A County District 11 RESIDENT and VOTER.
 What happened today at the Hamilton County Commission was shameful.
 Our District 11 School Board representative resigned with TWO YEARS remaining in the term. There was a path available that would have allowed District 11 voters to choose who represents us in the November election.
 Instead, the Commission chose not to take that path.
 Yes, I heard the discussion about the law going back to 1925.
 But don’t let the semantics fool you.
 Current Tennessee law also provides a path for an appointed School Board member to serve until a successor is elected and qualified.
 And we have a general election THIS NOVEMBER.
 The path was simple:
 1️⃣ Declare the seat vacant.
 ⬇️
 2️⃣ Make the temporary appointment.
 ⬇️
 3️⃣ Let the parties caucus.
 ⬇️
 4️⃣ Let independents qualify.
 ⬇️
 5️⃣ Put the candidates on the November ballot.
 ⬇️
 🗳️ LET. THE. PEOPLE. VOTE.
 That’s it.
 Clean. Simple. Easy.
 Instead, District 11 voters will not get to choose our School Board representative at the ballot box this November.
 And THAT is my problem.
 The real question is simple:
 If there was a lawful path to let the people vote, why was letting the people vote such a problem?
 👏🏾 Kudos to MY District 11 Commissioner Montrell Besley for standing up for the people he represents and supporting our opportunity to choose our representative.
 🚨 Warning shots fired.
 Because when politics begins to have more power than people, every voter should pay attention.
 Today it’s District 11.
 Tomorrow it could be your district.
 Whether you’re a Democrat, Republican, Independent, or none of the above, this should not be complicated:
 🗳️ OUR DISTRICT. OUR REPRESENTATIVE. WHY NOT OUR VOTE?
 ⚠️ POLITICS OVER PEOPLE IS NEVER OKAY.
 And as we navigate moments like this, I’m reminded of what Scripture requires of us:
 🙏🏾 “Act justly. Love mercy. Walk humbly with your God.” — Micah 6:8

 Spearheaded by Chattanooga Fire Department Captain Skyler Phillips, this custom farm-themed playground was designed with universal accessibility at its core, ensuring children of all physical abilities can play together without barriers.
 Event Details
 Date: September 12th
 Time: 10:00 AM
 Location: Jack Benson Heritage Park, 1428 Jenkins Road, Chattanooga, TN 37421
 Designed for ages 2–12, the park features fully ramped play structures, wheelchair-accessible carousel elements, adaptive swings, sensory enrichment stations, and seamless rubber surfacing for barrier-free play.
 Join local leaders, community partners, and neighbors for the ribbon-cutting to celebrate this vibrant new asset for families.

items.content_text:
We are deeply saddened by the passing of Shane Morrow, a dedicated community leader and visionary.
 Shane gave so much of his time, energy and heart to making Chattanooga a better place. Through his leadership and commitment to others, he touched countless lives and helped make our community stronger.
Shane Reynald Morrow, beloved life partner, musician, artist, community builder, helper, connector, and visionary, passed away August 26, 2026 at the age of 57.
 Born in Bridgeport, Connecticut, Shane was the son of the late Cheryl Morrow Tinsley and Larry Black. He graduated from Central High School in Bridgeport and continued his education at Housatonic Community College, where he completed a two-year program in computer programming.
 Shane was a musician at heart. Coming from generations of piano players, music was both a gift and a language through which he connected with others. But Shane's passion extended far beyond his own creativity. He believed deeply in the power of the arts to bring people together, preserve culture, create opportunity, and make communities stronger.
 Shane was, above all, a helper and a connector.
 He had a remarkable ability to see possibility in people, sometimes before they could see it in themselves. He connected artists to opportunities, people to resources, friends to one another, and ideas to the people who could help make them real. If someone needed help, Shane looked for a way to provide it. If someone had a gift that deserved to be seen, he looked for a stage. If there was a door that needed to be opened, Shane would open it.
 That spirit was at the heart of Jazzanooga, which Shane co-founded with his life partner, James McKissic. What began in 2011 as a celebration of Jazz Appreciation Month grew into an organization dedicated to celebrating Chattanooga's rich Black musical heritage, expanding access to the arts, and creating opportunities for artists and communities too often overlooked.
 Shane believed that the arts should belong to everyone. He worked to remove the financial, cultural, and social barriers that could prevent people from experiencing them. Under his leadership, Jazzanooga grew from a festival into a year-round community arts organization, eventually evolving into RISE Chattanooga, Responsive Initiatives for Social Empowerment.
 Through RISE, Shane's vision grew even broader. Music remained central, but so did entrepreneurship, cultural preservation, professional development for creatives, community empowerment, and creating opportunities for Black and Brown artists, businesses, and neighborhoods. Whether through a concert in a city park, a program for young musicians, support for a creative entrepreneur, or simply introducing two people who needed to know one another, Shane understood that building community was about building relationships.
 Shane's impact cannot be measured only by the organizations he founded, the programs he created, or the performances he helped bring to Chattanooga. His true legacy lives in people: the artists he encouraged, the young people he inspired, the entrepreneurs he supported, the friendships he nurtured, the introductions he made, the opportunities he created, and the many people he helped simply because helping was part of who he was.
 Shane was preceded in death by his parents, Cheryl Morrow Tinsley and Larry Black.
 He leaves behind his partner of nearly thirty years, James McKissic, his baby, Zora McKissic; his aunts and uncles Russel Ray, David Ray, Barney Ray, Mary Ray, Lance Morrow, Brent Morrow, Jason Morrow, Eugenia McCallister; and an extended network of cousins, friends, artists, musicians, colleagues, neighbors, and community members whose lives were enriched by Shane’s friendship, generosity, creativity, and care. 
 Shane believed that creativity could transcend barriers and that everyone deserved the opportunity to experience the joy, dignity, and connection that the arts can provide. He spent his life putting that belief into practice.
 The music, relationships, organizations, and community Shane helped build will continue. And in each person he connected to another, each artist he encouraged to step onto a stage, each idea he helped become reality, and each person he stopped to help along the way, a part of Shane remains.
 His was a life of creativity, service, connection, and love. And the community he spent so much of his life building will carry his spirit forward. 
 The community is invited to join family and friends of Shane Morrow in a celebration of his life through music and the arts on September 20, 2026, 4:00 pm at the Walker Theater in the Soldiers and Sailors Memorial Auditorium, 399 McCallie Avenue Chattanooga, TN 37402. In lieu of flowers, the family invites you to honor Shane’s memory with a donation to the Sankofa Fund for Civic Engagement. Donations will support youth music programs in Chattanooga, reflecting Shane’s love of music, the arts, and the importance of creating opportunities for young people in our community.
 To make a donation, please visit:
 https://cfgc.fcsuite.com/erp/donate
 Select “Sankofa Fund”, and follow the prompts to complete your gift.
 Your generosity is a meaningful way to celebrate Shane’s life and help carry forward his legacy through music and the arts
